snippet.title: Rebirth: The New Library of Alexandria
snippet.description:
Explorations in Science Old and New: A TV Series of 25-minute-episodes prepared and presented by Ismail Serageldin (available in Arabic and English)

50 Centuries of Science
This is the Story of Science in Egypt. It is the story of 50 centuries of science embracing astronomy, mathematics, engineering, medicine and many other fields, including the development of the modern empirical method a thousand years ago, centuries before the European Renaissance. And how, after a period of stagnation, Egypt re-igniting its talents to join in the 21st century enterprise of global knowledge.

REBIRTH: THE NEW LIBRARY OF ALEXANDRIA
Where the Ancient Library of Alexandria once stood, a beautiful new building has emerged. The dream of reviving that center of culture and learning has been realized. The Library came to life again. This is the story of how this one Egyptian project welcomes the new century, the century of science and informatics. It is the story of the rebirth of the fabled Bibliotheca Alexandrina, the New Library of Alexandria.

snippet.title: The Library of Alexandria: History’s Greatest Lost Knowledge | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
The Library of Alexandria is often described as the most ambitious center of knowledge in the ancient world.

Founded in the third century BCE, the library sought to collect and preserve texts from across civilizations, covering philosophy, science, medicine, mathematics, and literature. Yet despite its historical significance, no physical remains of the library have ever been definitively identified, and no complete record of its contents has survived.

This documentary examines what is known about the Library of Alexandria through ancient sources, historical context, and modern scholarship. It explores how the library functioned, the competing accounts of its decline, and why historians cannot agree on when or how its knowledge was lost.

Rather than focusing on legend or spectacle, this investigation addresses documented facts, conflicting testimonies, and the structural limitations that prevent definitive conclusions.

What was truly lost in Alexandria?
And how much of that loss can ever be measured?

snippet.title: The Great Library of Alexandria: The World’s First Research Center I SLICE HISTORY
snippet.description:
In the 4th century BC, when Alexander the Great discovered the place that would later become Alexandria, it was a simple fishing village on a coastal lagoon, surrounded by marshes.

Yet it was there that the conqueror, Alexander the Great set out to build the most dazzling and most cosmopolitan of ancient great cities. Built from nothing, the city with its perfectly geometric design, would rise as one gigantic block from the land, and become home to up to 1 million people. Its avant-garde style would revolutionise ancient urban design. Ideally situated between two "seas", between two worlds, between the East and the West, Alexandria would become the market place of the Mediterranean world. Its unique location would bring it great wealth and allow the building of incomparable structures: the Great Library, veritable centre of universal knowledge, the splendid Serapeum, and the monumental Lighthouse of Alexandria, ready to illuminate the world for centuries to come. Feast your eyes on a reconstruction of the mega-city and its amazing buildings. Once upon a time, Alexandria was built…

Directed by : Fabrice Hourlier

snippet.description:
Step into the legendary world of the Library of Alexandria, the most famous center of knowledge in the ancient world. In this cinematic 4K history documentary from Histouris, we explore the rise, glory, mysteries, and disappearance of the library that came to symbolize humanity’s greatest dream: collecting the knowledge of the known world under one roof.

Founded under the Ptolemaic dynasty in Alexandria, Egypt, the Library of Alexandria was more than a building filled with papyrus scrolls. It was part of a wider intellectual ecosystem linked to the Mouseion, a research center where scholars studied mathematics, astronomy, medicine, philosophy, geography, literature, and the natural world. It attracted thinkers from across the Mediterranean and helped turn Alexandria into one of antiquity’s greatest cities of learning.

But the story is not only about books. It is about power, memory, ambition, and fragility. How did one library become the most enduring symbol of lost knowledge? How many scrolls did it really hold? Was it destroyed in a single fire, or did it fade through repeated damage, political upheaval, and institutional decline? Why does its loss still feel personal in the modern age?

This documentary follows the real historical debate. Ancient and modern sources connect the library to the early Ptolemies, likely around the reign of Ptolemy I and Ptolemy II, and later accounts connect at least some destruction to Julius Caesar’s Alexandrian War in 48 BCE. Yet historians continue to debate the scale of that event and whether parts of the library survived afterward. Other evidence suggests the story of destruction was gradual, unfolding in stages across later centuries rather than ending in one single night.

In this episode, we reconstruct ancient Alexandria: its royal quarter, harbor, scholars’ halls, scribes, papyrus archives, and the atmosphere of a city where curiosity itself was a form of power. We also explore the names and ideas associated with Alexandria’s intellectual world, from Eratosthenes and Callimachus to Euclid and Aristarchus, while separating legend from evidence wherever possible.

The Library of Alexandria remains one of the greatest symbols of human ambition ever imagined: a place where rulers sought prestige through knowledge, and where the loss of memory became one of history’s most haunting warnings.

snippet.title: They Hid Africa’s First Library The Truth About Alexandria & Timbuktu
snippet.description:
African history, Black history, Timbuktu, and ancient Egypt — this documentary uncovers the truth they never taught you: the world’s first great libraries weren’t Greek or European… they were African.
Before Alexandria’s marble halls rose, the temples of Kemet (Ancient Egypt), Kush, and Timbuktu were already archiving science, medicine, philosophy, and astronomy. This is the hidden story of how Africa built the foundations of world civilization — and how that truth was buried by empire and conquest.
For thousands of years, the Nile Valley and the Sahara were networks of universities: temples at Heliopolis, Thebes, and Memphis where priests studied geometry, medicine, and the stars. Their scrolls inspired Greece. Their teachings became “philosophy.” And when Europe claimed the Library of Alexandria as the cradle of learning, it was really inheriting Africa’s genius.
Centuries later, as Egypt faded, that flame moved west — to Timbuktu, the jewel of Mali. Home to Sankoré University, over 700,000 manuscripts, and scholars who debated science and spirituality while Europe called Africa “dark.”
This documentary connects Kemet, Kush, Carthage, and Timbuktu — proving that Africa didn’t borrow civilization; it built it. The Great Library of Africa never died — it was buried, and now we’re uncovering it.

How ancient Egypt’s temple-universities inspired Greek philosophy


The real origins of the Library of Alexandria and why it was African


The rise of Kush and the continuation of Nile Valley knowledge


How the wisdom of Kemet flowed into Mali and Timbuktu
